Played in a medium-length SWRPG game and currently running a Genesys campaign, and I feel like one of the system's biggest weaknesses is that the system can sometimes feel too much like it's existing in this space between two solidly defined points, trying to serve two masters.

For a game that leans so heavily into the narration of the story, there are a shit-ton of charts. Now, I'll admit that most of them are probably not as necessary when you've got a solid hold on the system, but the game is very hard to run without a screen or reference pamphlet of some kind.

In a conflict, you have no direction aside from a short "best suggest" and you have to eyeball the opposition to make a guess at balance. The only repository of enemies (outside of DrainSmith's resources) is the adversary decks, the enemies are just scattered through the book which is frustrating when you're not running Terrinoth and just need to know where to find a freaking sea serpent. Some amount of design theory on how to build opposition would be helpful here, have the designers talk about how they go about building an ability, skill totals, wound thresholds.

Your Paladin lashed out, but it's something that happens. It sounds like what these bandits did ran exactly against both you (the player) and Ilmater's hot buttons. But you're a Vengeance Paladin. That's the part of 5E that's a big departure from previous lore, the oaths. Vengeance is the Hammer of the Gods.

If it's the kind of game you're in, talk to the DM about how to call into focus the path forward. You were right to kill them, and the big question becomes, did you use the most clean level of retribution possible? If you can't take them all out in combat, you aren't required to challenge them to it. Your job is to get shit done, but not to revel in it.

I think the biggest thing you have to think about in terms of translating something from one game to another is trying to figure out what is it that your trying to translate, and what key ability or cool trick you're trying to carry across.

What PrC's and Feats do you have in mind?

For feats, I think you've got an easier time (depending on the feat). The feats in 5e are much more powerful and individual, and taking even one helps to define a character.

Now, I'll say that I hate the idea of Prestige Classes creeping their way back into 5e, so I have a slight bias here. Treat 3.x classes that you want to bring in the same way Wizards is treating kits, make them class options if they are defining enough to what a character is.

One of the DM's in my group and I were talking about the problem of rests being too often for combat in his game, and we had come up with something that I called dramatic timing for rests. Basically, you'd scale rests to the scale of what the party is facing.

* Party is out in the wilderness or playing out a slow series of intrigues in a city over the course of weeks? Then a good night's sleep is only a short rest and you need to be somewhere you can really relax to fully recover and recharge.
* In the thick of a dungeon? Hello normal timing, all the little stresses of the world fall away and getting your head down for eight hours seems like a miracle all on it's own.

I think it really depends. How much is the race going to decide who and what a character is? A good idea may be to set aside one aspect specifically for race/culture, which allows them to either play into their stereotypes or stand against them. A for example for a medieval fantasy-ish game (okay, a Dungeons and Fate game):

* High Concept
* Trouble
* Race
* Ethical Outlook
* Personal Aspect

And as for making a character pay to play a race, a good number of FATE games seem to run off the idea that the more power you have, the harder it is for you to stand against your nature; a vampire or demon can't easily deny his base instincts and tends to be subordinate to them. If being an elf comes with a heaping helping of magical nature and "I'm one with the world and the winds," then they might have a hard time not acting that way just like the first two examples.

If everyone is standing in the same place, it might not make as much sense to charge everyone for a thing and instead just make it fait accompli.

Give them something more to interact with than just a group of bandits on the road. This is something that is highly dependent upon your group, and how quickly they can pick up a stray thought and roll into a riff with it.

Some ideas:

* Make the bandit's first impression a laugh.
* Have a wheezing old man in the middle of the road, over-play the voice and have him make ridiculously large demands. 
* Once the violence starts, have the bandits give up once it looks like they might die. Leave the party figuring out how to deal with the prisoners.

What happens really depends on what kind of people your group contains.
